title: 2025-03-11 Redwood Private VPC Security Architecture Deep Dive with Meridian Bank
next_steps: Send SOC 2 Type II report and ISO27001 evidence
Share detailed network diagram and suggested firewall ruleset
Schedule follow-up to review audit log format and retention (week of 2025-03-18)
Run short network connectivity test between Meridian VPC and Redwood Private staging environment
action_items: Owner: Lina Gomez | Item: Share initial Redwood Private architecture diagram and VPC peering / PrivateLink options | Due: 2025-03-18
Owner: Marcus Reed | Item: Provide Meridian CIDR ranges and proxy/firewall egress point details | Due: 2025-03-14
Owner: Sanjay Patel | Item: Send SOC2 report, ISO evidence, and KMS/HSM integration notes | Due: 2025-03-12
summary: Deep dive on private VPC/on-prem architecture for Meridian Bank: covered network isolation, ingress/egress controls, firewalling, SSO/RBAC integration, audit logs and encryption/KMS. Action items include sharing architecture diagrams, SOC2 artifacts and scheduling a follow-up network test.
meeting_header: Date: 2025-03-11 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 62 minutes | Redwood: Sanjay Patel (AE), Lina Gomez (SE) | Meridian: Karen Liu (CISO), Marcus Reed (Infra Lead), Nadia Khan (Cloud Security)
transcript: [00:00] Sanjay Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Karen Liu: Karen here, CISO at Meridian. Hello.
[00:09] Marcus Reed: Marcus, infra lead, hi.
[00:11] Nadia Khan: Nadia, cloud security. Good afternoon.
[00:15] Sanjay Patel: Great. Lina from our SE team will lead the architecture deep dive. Lina?

[00:20] Lina Gomez: Thanks, Sanjay. Hi team. Our goal today is to walk through Redwood Private deployed into a customer VPC or on-prem, talk network isolation, ingress/egress, firewalling, and the security controls around keys, logs, and SSO. I'll flag where we commonly see questions.
[00:36] Marcus Reed: Quick note - we're evaluating both VPC peering and PrivateLink approaches. We need minimal egress and want full control over outbound firewalling.

[00:44] Lina Gomez: Totally. We support two primary patterns: 1) Redwood Private inside your VPC via our private endpoint and service mesh, typically using VPC endpoints/PrivateLink; 2) air-gapped on-prem package for highly regulated setups. For VPC flow we can do no-internet egress for model inference - egress only to customer-managed S3 or to allowed outbound proxies.
[01:05] Nadia Khan: When you say "no-internet egress," do you mean all outbound traffic can be routed through our NAT/proxy and blocked at our firewall?

[01:11] Lina Gomez: Yes, we can have the compute nodes in a private subnet with a route to your NAT gateway. Outbound only via your egress. We also support establishing IP allowlists if you have fixed IP ranges on Redwood side for callbacks, though in many cases we prefer PrivateLink so you don't have to open inbound rules at all.
[01:28] Karen Liu: Need to understand ingress - do you require any inbound from Redwood control plane? We want minimal inbound and strict auditability.

[01:34] Sanjay Patel: Good question. For Redwood Private there's an optional control plane connection. For VPC-deployed Private, the control plane can be customer-managed or we can use a private control plane with no public endpoints. If you choose air-gapped, control plane is fully customer-managed. We'll provide a list of endpoints and certs for any control-plane telemetry.
[01:52] Marcus Reed: Can you share those endpoints and the cert rotation cadence? Our security policy mandates cert rotation every 90 days and keys managed in our HSM.

[01:58] Lina Gomez: We'll share the endpoint list post-call. For certs we support mutual TLS between control plane and runtime; rotation frequency can be aligned to your policy. For KMS - we integrate with customer KMS via IAM roles and can use customer-managed keys. We also support HSM-backed keys if you require FIPS/HSM protections.
[02:18] Nadia Khan: How's key lifecycle handled? Is Redwood storing plaintext keys?

[02:21] Sanjay Patel: We never store customer plaintext keys. We use envelope encryption. Customer-managed KMS wraps the data keys; Redwood stores only encrypted blobs. In air-gapped deployments keys can stay on your HSM and never leave your network.
[02:34] Karen Liu: Audit logs - we need immutable logs for access and admin actions with at least 1 year retention and export to our SIEM. How does Redwood support that?

[02:42] Lina Gomez: We emit audit events for admin actions, API calls, model rollouts, and key operations. For Private VPC we can stream logs to your logging endpoint (e.g., syslog, Kinesis, or direct to S3) using signed uploads or a customer-side collector. We also support JSON schema that maps to our audit fields; we'll send sample schemas.
[03:00] Marcus Reed: Any chance the event fields will mismatch our SIEM expectations? We have some parsing rules already in place.
[03:04] Lina Gomez: There might be minor differences - we've found customers ingest raw JSON and map fields. We'll provide a mapping guide and a sample log file so your SIEM team can test parsers.
[03:15] Karen Liu: SOC 2 / ISO - we've requested Redwood's evidence. Is that the standard SOC2 Type II and ISO27001 certificates?

[03:20] Sanjay Patel: Yes, we'll share SOC 2 Type II report and our ISO27001 certificate. For sensitive items we offer an NDA process - but our standard sales security pack includes SOC 2 bridge letter, controls matrix, and penetration test summary.
[03:33] Nadia Khan: On network firewalling: what ports need to be open inbound? Outbound? We're very strict and prefer explicit port lists.

[03:38] Lina Gomez: For PrivateLink the inbound is effectively handled by the VPC endpoint - no public inbound needed. For peering or direct IPs we provide the exact ephemeral port ranges for kernels/metrics. Generally, we ask for: outbound TCP 443 to control-plane endpoints if you allow managed control-plane; or no outbound if you host control-plane locally. We will provide a hardened port matrix - we'll share that as part of the deliverables.
[03:59] Marcus Reed: What about model downloads/updates? They can be heavy traffic; do those go through our egress?

[04:04] Lina Gomez: Yes, model artifacts can be pulled via your artifact store or via a signed transfer; in some setups we pre-stage model weights in a customer bucket to avoid internet pulls. That ensures model downloads stay within your network and you control the egress and auditing.
[04:19] Karen Liu: RBAC and SSO - we use SAML SSO with SCIM provisioning. Integration work?

[04:24] Sanjay Patel: Redwood supports SAML-based SSO and SCIM for user provisioning and group sync. For Private deployments you can bind to your IdP directly. We also support role mapping to onboard RBAC policies (e.g., admin, deployer, auditor).
[04:36] Nadia Khan: How are service accounts handled? We need least privilege for machine-to-machine creds, and rotation every 30 days ideally.

[04:41] Lina Gomez: Service accounts can be short-lived tokens minted by the control plane, and we integrate with your KMS for signing. Token TTLs are configurable and can be aligned to your rotation cadence. We'll share a sample token lifecycle diagram.
[04:53] Marcus Reed: Are there any known telemetry or metrics that leave the VPC?

[04:58] Lina Gomez: Metrics can be routed to your telemetry stack. By default we try not to push telemetry externally unless you opt-in to hosted dashboards. For Private we can route to customer collectors and disable external telemetry. There may be product health pings to the control plane unless you choose fully air-gapped mode.
[05:12] Karen Liu: We need to ensure egress filtering prevents data exfil via model completions or callbacks. Any built-in safeguards?

[05:18] Lina Gomez: You can disable external callbacks and webhooks; callbacks can be routed to your internal endpoints only. We also have response redaction options and can run output filters - but those are not a replacement for network filtering. We'll show the configuration for blocking outbound requests from runtime containers.
[05:33] Sanjay Patel: Also, for high-sensitivity customers we provide sidecar egress proxies that enforce allowlists and URL filtering at the process level.
[05:40] Nadia Khan: Sidecar proxy - is that Envoy? Does it support mTLS?
[05:43] Lina Gomez: We typically use Envoy with mTLS to your upstream proxies, yes. It's fully configurable and can perform SPIFFE-style identity if you want workload identity integrated.
[05:54] Marcus Reed: Logging retention - can we set retention to one year and have immutable storage?

[05:58] Lina Gomez: Yes - logs can be forwarded to your S3 with object lock / WORM if you need immutability. We don't enforce retention ourselves; you control it in your storage. We can also sign log files and include tamper-evidence headers.
[06:12] Karen Liu: How granular are audit events? We need to see token minting, model access, admin role changes, and export of logs showing user IDs and IPs.

[06:19] Lina Gomez: Events include actor, actor_type (user/service), event_type, resource, timestamp, request_id, source_ip, and outcome. We'll share the event schema. Some of the fields are best-effort if runtime can't see a source IP (e.g., if behind a proxy) - but in VPC deployments you can surface the client IP.
[06:36] Sanjay Patel: Quick aside - we sometimes see transcription autos replacing KV cache with KV cash, so apologies in materials. We'll make sure docs are clean.
[06:43] Karen Liu: Ha, noted. On data residency: our workloads must remain in-region (US East). Does Redwood guarantee region pinning?

[06:49] Lina Gomez: Yes, you can pin model execution and storage to a specific region in Redwood Private. For Dedicated we also have region controls. We'll include region-binding steps in the deployment guide.
[06:58] Marcus Reed: Network connectivity modes - list them so I can compare: VPC PrivateLink, VPC peering, Site-to-Site VPN/IPSec, Direct Connect/ExpressRoute, and on-prem offline install?
[07:07] Lina Gomez: Correct. For secure low-latency we recommend PrivateLink or Direct Connect. For air-gapped we do an on-prem package with an installation runbook.
[07:15] Nadia Khan: Does the on-prem package require internet for license checks or updates?

[07:19] Lina Gomez: No, on-prem can be fully offline. Updates are via signed bundles you fetch internally. License validation can be periodic and handled via a signed token exchange - all offline-capable.
[07:29] Karen Liu: Can you talk about process for vulnerability disclosures and patching windows? We need an SLA for critical patches.

[07:34] Sanjay Patel: We have a defined security response process. Critical CVEs are triaged and patches have an expedited window (often 24-72 hours for critical depending on customer environment). We'll include the security process doc in the pack.
[07:46] Marcus Reed: Any specific firewall rules examples you can show? For example, if we use PrivateLink, we only need to allow outbound HTTPS to the VPC endpoint DNS?

[07:55] Lina Gomez: Exactly. For PrivateLink you allow HTTPS to the VPC endpoint - ports 443 and mTLS on some control paths. If you opt for peering, we'll provide a specific set of IP CIDRs and ephemeral port ranges to allow between subnets.
[08:07] Nadia Khan: How do you handle internal lateral movement prevention? If an attacker lands on a runtime node, can they reach the control plane or other customer data?

[08:15] Lina Gomez: We isolate workloads by tenant at the process and kernel level, and we run runtime processes in constrained containers. Network policies enforce strict intra-subnet rules; cross-tenant comms are blocked. For high assurance, we recommend host-level hardening and running in your VPC so you control routing.
[08:29] Karen Liu: SLA on logging delivery? We need logs within 5 minutes typically for alerts.
[08:33] Lina Gomez: We aim for near-real-time streaming; typical delivery is under 30s to your collector. We'll validate during the pilot.
[08:41] Sanjay Patel: Ok let's surface a few items we'll send: SOC2 artifacts, architecture diagram, port matrix, audit event schema, KMS/HSM integration notes, and a sample log file.
[08:51] Karen Liu: And one more - are there any known perf tradeoffs when enabling full auditing and sidecar proxies? We have latency SLOs of 50ms p95.

[08:58] Lina Gomez: Good question. Sidecar proxies add a small p95 overhead (5-15ms typical). Audit logging to local buffer has negligible runtime CPU impact, but pushing logs off-host can add latency if synchronous. We recommend async log shipping and batching to keep p95 in range. For very tight SLOs we can do local KV caching and async flushes.
[09:17] Marcus Reed: On encryption at rest - aside from KMS, do you support customer-side encryption for model artifacts?
[09:22] Lina Gomez: Yes - you can store model artifacts in your bucket encrypted with your CMK. Redwood can access via IAM role; no plaintext is stored by Redwood.
[09:29] Nadia Khan: Can we rotate keys without downtime?
[09:31] Sanjay Patel: Key rotation is designed to be transparent via envelope keys. Rotation of the CMK should be seamless; we'll validate your rotation policy in staging.
[09:40] Karen Liu: What about admin access controls for model rollouts? We need approval gating and audit trails.
[09:45] Lina Gomez: We have role-based workflows and can require multi-approver rollouts. Each action is logged with who approved and a reason field - that shows up in the audit events.
[09:56] Marcus Reed: Can we do a quick walkthrough of a sample network diagram?

[10:00] Lina Gomez: I'll share my screen and show a diagram - but I'll verbally summarize: customer VPC with private subnets hosting Redwood runtime nodes; optional NAT in a public subnet for egress you control; VPC endpoint for control plane traffic; a logging collector in a separate subnet; and an optional sidecar/envoy for egress filtering. Models staged in customer S3 with CMK encryption. Control plane either in your VPC or in a private control plane - arrows all internal.
[10:24] Karen Liu: Any notes about traffic inspection tools? We use a TLS-inspecting proxy at the egress; will mutual TLS interfere?

[10:31] Lina Gomez: If you're doing TLS inspection, you can deploy the proxy inline and have the sidecar talk to it over mTLS; just ensure certs and trust chain are managed. We recommend not terminating mTLS at the proxy unless you can re-encrypt to the destination.
[10:44] Nadia Khan: On the topic of user provisioning via SCIM - can group sync map to RBAC roles automatically?
[10:49] Lina Gomez: Yes, our SCIM implementation supports group-to-role mapping. You can configure mappings so that the 'security' group becomes 'auditor' role in Redwood.
[10:58] Marcus Reed: A practical ask - send minimal firewall rule set we need for PrivateLink and peering.
[11:03] Sanjay Patel: We'll include that. Also adding for next steps: set up a staging environment pinned to us-east-1 with sample traffic so you can validate SLOs.
[11:11] Karen Liu: About incident response - in the event of suspected data exposure, what's the process?

[11:16] Sanjay Patel: Incident response involves immediate containment, audit log collection, and a joint post-mortem. We have an incident response team and will provide contact channels and SLAs in the security pack.
[11:27] Nadia Khan: Does Redwood produce MD5/SHA hashes for model artifacts for integrity verification?

[11:31] Lina Gomez: We produce signed checksums and can integrate with your artifact verification process. For on-prem air-gapped installs we provide signed bundles with signatures you can verify offline.
[11:41] Marcus Reed: Any limitations for high-throughput inference when sidecars and logging are enabled?

[11:45] Lina Gomez: Throughput impact is minimal if proxies are scaled appropriately; we'll help size the runtime and recommend batching configs. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization and batching to keep cost and latency acceptable.
[11:58] Karen Liu: We need to vet the supply chain too - do you provide SBOMs for runtime images?
[12:03] Lina Gomez: Yes, we can provide SBOMs and base image lists for the runtime. We'll include those in the materials.

[12:11] Sanjay Patel: Ok folks, wrapping up, I'll send the security pack and Lina will share the diagram and lattice of firewall rules. Marcus, if you can send CIDR ranges and egress proxy details, Lina will draft the network playbook.
[12:24] Marcus Reed: Will do. Expect email by tomorrow.
[12:27] Karen Liu: Thanks everyone. One last question - demonstration of log schema and sample entry would be great in the next call.
[12:33] Lina Gomez: We'll include a sample JSON log and schedule the follow-up deep-dive on logs. Thanks all.
[12:38] Sanjay Patel: Thanks - action items recap in email. Meeting adjourned.
[12:42] (call ends)
